doc.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: Early jazz as art; the Nighthawks
title: Black and white bands in the 1920s
summary: He sees a difference in freedom to play jazz between black and white bands, with white players learning from black ones.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: And for your ears is there a discernable difference between the black bands and the white bands going back as far as you do?

Yeah, oh yeah. I think they basically were fulfilling the same obligation of dance music, popular music. I think the black bands really did have a little bit more freedom in playing jazz than the white musicians. A lot of the white musicians, of course you know, respected and learned about jazz from their black musician friends, the countless stories of the Austin High Gang fellows going down to hear King Oliver and buying the recordings and studying and copying. And I think there was a lot of cross pollenization. A lot of bands and musicians worked together, you know, and which were learning from each other. It was a great learning session. But yet there was a difference.
